title: Slide IR
description: The neutral contract between every input adapter (HTML, AI author) and the deterministic renderer. An author -- human, Claude, Codex or Gemini -- emits ONLY this. It never emits PPTX, OOXML, DrawingML, coordinates, fonts or colours: those are the template's job. Block types are derived from the real 30-slide corpus, not invented.

ir_version.description: Bump on any breaking change; the renderer refuses versions it does not know.

deck.description: Deck-level metadata. In the HTML corpus this comes from the .hero block, which sits OUTSIDE the .card sections -- it is not a slide, it is the deck header, and the renderer turns it into the title slide.

language.description: Drives which content budget applies. Korean glyphs are full-width: a box holding 60 Latin chars holds ~31 Hangul. 'mixed' budgets against the CJK (pessimistic) figure.

source.description: Provenance: the HTML filename, or the prompt/topic for an AI-authored deck.

id.description: Stable handle for QA feedback (e.g. 'slide-07'). The visual-QA loop reports defects against this id.

layout_id.description: MUST be a layout name that exists in reference/layout_manifest.json. The renderer resolves it against the template's OWN slide_layouts and calls add_slide(layout). An unknown layout_id is a hard validation failure -- never a silently-substituted default, because a silent substitution produces a plausible-looking but off-brand deck.

title.description: Fills the layout's TITLE placeholder. The hard cap here is a runaway-output guard only; the REAL limit is the per-layout content budget in the manifest, enforced by render/fit.py.

notes.description: Speaker notes. Free of budget constraints -- the notes pane scrolls.

blocks.description: Body content, in reading order. The renderer maps blocks onto the layout's non-title placeholders in order, then onto free-floating shapes once placeholders run out.

block.description: Closed union, discriminated on `type`. Every member is traceable to a construct that actually occurs in the corpus.

heading.description: An <h3> inside a card: a sub-section header grouping the bullets under it. 28 occurrences in the corpus -- common enough to be first-class, and flattening it into a bold bullet loses the visual hierarchy.

paragraph.description:
The lead

under the

. Sets up the slide in one sentence.

bullets.description: A <ul>. 22 occurrences. Nesting is capped at 3 levels because the template's body placeholder only styles lvl1-lvl3 legibly.

callout.description: The corpus has THREE callout variants, not one: .alert-box (4x, neutral/key-message), .warn-box (2x, risk) and .ok-box (1x, confirmation). They differ only in accent colour, so one block type with a `variant` discriminator is the right shape -- the renderer picks the fill/left-bar colour from the theme.

table.description: 11 occurrences -- the single densest block in the corpus and the one most likely to overflow. Cells are rich text because the corpus routinely puts inline <code> in them (API signature tables).

columns.description: Capped at 6: beyond that a 13.3in slide cannot render legible cells.

rows.description: Every row MUST have exactly len(columns) cells. JSON Schema cannot express that cross-field constraint; models.py enforces it.

code.description: A <pre><code> block. Only 2 occur in the corpus -- but one of those is the tabbed C++/C# pair in Slide Template.html (.tabs/.tab-content), so `variants` is required to model it. PowerPoint has no tab control, so the renderer emits either side-by-side boxes or consecutive slides; that choice is the renderer's, not the author's.

image.description: 3 occurrences, all image/jpeg data-URIs (NOT png -- verified against the corpus). The adapter decodes base64 -> BytesIO -> add_picture. `alt` is mandatory: it is what the AI author sees when it re-reads a deck, and what the visual-QA critic checks the placement against.

kind.description: data_uri: 'data:image/jpeg;base64,...' straight out of the HTML. path: relative to the IR file, for AI-authored decks that reference real assets.

diagram.description: 3 .mermaid blocks (1 sequenceDiagram, 2 flowcharts) plus 1 hand-drawn inline SVG. The AI author emits mermaid source ONLY -- it is a text format the model is fluent in, and it keeps the 'AI never emits geometry' invariant intact. render/diagrams.py decides how to realise it.

kind.description: Lets the renderer pick a strategy without re-parsing the source.

render_hint.description: native = editable PowerPoint autoshapes (only viable for simple linear/flowchart graphs); image = rasterise via mermaid-cli and drop in a picture; auto = let diagrams.py decide by node count. See foundation_research.md S7.

steps.description: .step-badge, 10 occurrences -- a numbered process sequence. Distinct from `bullets`: the order is semantic and the renderer draws numbered chevrons, not dots.

cards.description: .mini-card (9x) laid out in .grid-2/.grid-3 (4x), often carrying a .tag (8x). A row of peer concepts -- renders as N side-by-side rounded rectangles. Also the target for .photo-grid/.photo-placeholder once its is lifted out into an `image` block.

rich_text.description: Inline formatting. Inline <code> occurs 111 times in the corpus -- by a wide margin the most common inline mark -- so run-level styling is NOT optional: flattening it to plain text would visibly degrade every API slide. Two accepted forms: a bare string (the common case, and the one an LLM gets right most reliably), or an explicit run array. models.py normalises the string form into a single unstyled run.
